title: New Grub Street: A Literary Discussion

utterances.text: Welcome to New Grub Street Unpacked, a podcast devoted to one of the great unread masterpieces of Victorian fiction.
George Gissing published New Grub Street in 1891, and it remains one of the most unflinching portraits of literary life ever written.
It is a novel about writers who cannot write, about the marketplace that devours them, and about the impossible question of what art is worth when the rent is due.
To help us unpack it, I have three extraordinary companions around the table today.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing professor whose great passion is how fiction is actually constructed — the machinery behind the sentences.
If there's a structural choice in this novel that rewards attention, Eleanor will find it.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who brings the real world crashing into the text — what poverty actually meant, what the literary marketplace actually did to people.
He has a gift for dry anger, which will serve us well with this novel.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read New Grub Street as a teenager and has returned to it so many times she practically knows it by heart.
She will tell us what it feels like to read this book — and that, I think, is where we should begin.
The novel opens with Jasper Milvain at breakfast, watching a funeral procession pass the window, and immediately calculating whether there's a journalistic angle in it.
From that first page, Gissing announces his great theme: the collision between art and the market.
James, I want to start with you, because Jasper Milvain makes his philosophy absolutely explicit very early in the novel.
What is Gissing doing when he gives Jasper these extraordinary speeches about the literary marketplace?
What Gissing is doing, I think, is a kind of controlled provocation.
He puts the most ruthlessly honest account of the literary economy into the mouth of the character we are most tempted to enjoy.
Jasper is charming, funny, astute — and he is also the villain of the piece.
The key passage for me is where Jasper lays out his entire commercial philosophy without a trace of embarrassment.
He says: 'To please the vulgar you must, one way or another, incarnate the genius of vulgarity.'
Now, that phrase — 'incarnate the genius of vulgarity' — is not a dismissal of commercial writing.
It is, perversely, a kind of tribute to it.
Jasper is saying that selling out takes skill, takes craft — it is not something a fool can manage.
And that is a deeply uncomfortable argument, because it is not entirely wrong.
What strikes me about that passage is its structural bravado.
Gissing gives Jasper this perfectly constructed little manifesto, and it reads almost like a parody of a Victorian essay.
The rhythm of it — the qualifications, the 'mind you,' the casual 'for my own part' — all of that performs the very confidence it describes.
Jasper is demonstrating his cleverness at the same moment he is explaining his cleverness.
He even admits he cannot reach 'the bulkiest multitude' — that is a marvellous phrase — and turns it into a compliment to himself.
He targets the upper middle class of intellect — people who cannot, as he says, distinguish between stones and paste.
It is a portrait of a man who has perfectly calibrated his ambitions to the available market, and Gissing admires the precision of that even as he condemns it.
What I keep coming back to is how seductive Jasper is as a narrator of his own life.
When you are inside one of his speeches, you almost agree with him.
And then you step back and realise that the character standing opposite him — Edwin Reardon — will eventually be destroyed by everything Jasper so cheerfully endorses.
Reardon articulates the human cost of that market with heartbreaking precision.
There is a passage where he says: 'The world has no pity on a man who can't do or produce something it thinks worth money.'
And then he goes further: 'Society is as blind and brutal as fate.'
Those two sentences together are everything the novel is about.
Jasper has made his peace with that blindness and brutality — and Reardon simply cannot.
And Gissing does not let Reardon off the hook entirely, which is what makes the novel so honest.
Reardon himself says 'I have no right to complain of my own ill-fortune; it's my own fault in a sense.'
That parenthetical 'in a sense' is doing an enormous amount of work.
It is the sound of a man trying to be fair to a system that is not being fair to him.
What Gissing understood, with the precision of someone who had lived it, is that structural disadvantage and individual failure are not mutually exclusive.
You can be both the victim of an unjust system and a man who was not equipped to survive it.
That is the trap of Grub Street, and Gissing refuses to simplify it.
There is a moment in Chapter 31 where the narrator steps forward and says something extraordinary about Reardon and his friend Harold Biffen directly.
Gissing drops the fiction of detachment and simply argues on their behalf.
The narrator says: 'These two were richly endowed with the kindly and the imaginative virtues; if fate threw them amid incongruous circumstances, is their endowment of less value?'
That rhetorical question is a rebuke aimed directly at the reader.
Gissing is asking whether we have absorbed Jasper's values without realising it — whether we too judge a man by his market value.
The novel is, among other things, a sustained argument against that way of measuring a human life.
And that passage about passivity — 'You scorn their passivity; but it was their nature and their merit to be passive' — I find that almost unbearably moving.
Because Gissing is not defending laziness.
He is defending a particular kind of temperament — gentle, imaginative, ill-suited to combat — that the world will always punish.
And what is devastating is that he wrote these characters from the inside.
This is not a sociologist's account of literary poverty — it is a wounded man's testimony.
A wounded man's testimony — that is the phrase I want to carry into the rest of this conversation.
Because it raises the question at the heart of the novel's second great story: not Jasper's glittering ascent, but Edwin Reardon's very precise and very painful collapse.
In our next segment, we look closely at the architecture of that decline — how Gissing builds it, sentence by sentence, choice by choice, until it becomes almost unbearable to watch.

segments.title: The Architecture of Decline: Reardon's Spiral

utterances.text: We've been talking about the trap of Grub Street — the marketplace that crushes the literary ideal.
Now I want to turn to the man caught most visibly in its teeth: Edwin Reardon, and the extraordinary portrait Gissing draws of a writer in free fall.
What strikes me first about Gissing's treatment of Reardon is that the decline is architectural — it has a structure, a sequence, almost a terrible logic.
There's a passage in Chapter Six where Reardon diagnoses himself with remarkable precision — and Gissing lets him do it in his own voice, which is a bold choice.
He says, and I want to read this carefully:
'A temperament like mine can't pass through such a violent change of conditions without being greatly affected; I have never since been the man I was before I left England.'
That phrase — 'never since been the man I was' — is doing something almost clinical.
Reardon is performing his own post-mortem while still alive, and Gissing trusts us to feel the horror of that.
It's worth pausing on what Reardon means by that 'violent change of conditions,' because it's not simply emotional upheaval.

He goes abroad, returns, marries Amy — and suddenly he is no longer writing from a position of disciplined privation but from within a household that has expectations, costs, a social surface to maintain.
The market doesn't merely depress the writer's income — it infiltrates the conditions of his labour, his domestic arrangements, his very sense of what he owes the people who depend on him.
Reardon ends that same speech by saying: 'But the due course of things is troubled by my poverty.'
'But the due course of things is troubled by my poverty.'
Seven words that carry the whole weight of the novel's argument.
And the body registers it before the mind admits it.
There's a passage in Chapter Fifteen that I find almost unbearable to read, because Gissing renders the physical wreckage so precisely.
He writes:
'The past twelve months had added several years to Edwin Reardon's seeming age; at thirty-three he would generally have been taken for forty.'
Thirty-three and taken for forty.
That gap of seven years is the price Grub Street has extracted from his body — not just his bank account.
And then Gissing adds: 'Ceaseless perplexity and dread gave a wandering, sometimes a wild, expression to his eyes.'
'Ceaseless perplexity and dread gave a wandering, sometimes a wild, expression to his eyes.'
That word 'wild' hits very hard when you've been watching this man try to hold himself together.
What Gissing does so brilliantly — and I think this is underappreciated — is show the decline at the level of the sentence, inside Reardon's actual writing.
There's a scene in Chapter Nine that is almost comic in its horror — Reardon at the desk, his prose disintegrating in real time.
Gissing gives us these ghastly examples of what Reardon actually produces:
'She took a book with a look of—' or 'A revision of this decision would have made him an object of derision.'
Those are actual samples of what exhausted syntax produces — the rhymes and echoes of a mind that can no longer control its material.
And then comes this terrible little declaration: 'I can't help it; it must go; the time is passing.'
'I can't help it; it must go; the time is passing.'
He submits bad work knowingly, and that knowing is the worst part.
Which connects directly to the question of professional integrity under commercial pressure — a question Gissing frames in surprisingly direct terms.
There's a passage in Chapter Four where Reardon articulates exactly what separates him from the Milvains of his world.
He calls it — and this phrase has stayed with me —
'the shrinking from conscious insincerity of workmanship — which most of the writers nowadays seem never to feel.'
'Conscious insincerity of workmanship' — that is a precise and damning phrase.
It means knowing your work is bad and submitting it anyway because the market will accept it.
Reardon can't do it — and that inability is both his moral distinction and his commercial death sentence.
The marriage mirrors the work, doesn't it?
The same process of silent erosion — the same inability to say the thing that would save it.
In Chapter Twelve, Gissing describes what has happened between Reardon and Amy with a precision that is almost surgical.
'Their relations to each other — not long ago an inexhaustible topic — would not bear spoken comment; both were too conscious of the danger-signal when they looked that way.'
'The danger-signal.' As if there's a whole railway system of catastrophe waiting if they let the conversation go somewhere honest.
And the tragedy is that Reardon can see it — he sees the coldness forming in himself, he watches it happen — but he cannot stop it.
That self-awareness is Gissing's cruelest gift to Reardon.
By Chapter Thirty-One, that awareness has curdled into something almost philosophical — and I think it's one of the most startling speeches in the novel.
Reardon says:
'To have had even a small reputation, and to have outlived it, is a sort of anticipation of death.'
'The man Edwin Reardon, whose name was sometimes spoken in a tone of interest, is really and actually dead.'
'And what remains of me is resigned to that. I have an odd fancy that it will make death itself easier; it is as if only half of me had now to die.'
'Only half of me had now to die' — he has already performed the amputation himself, spiritually.
That is Gissing at his very finest: a character who has thought his way so clearly into his own ruin that he finds a kind of cold comfort there.
The man who can see his own decline with that clarity — and yet cannot arrest it.
It makes Reardon both a tragic figure and, in a strange way, one of the most lucid minds in the novel.

And that lucidity throws the novel's other great intelligence into very sharp relief — because next we turn to the man who is watching all of this and drawing entirely different conclusions: Jasper Milvain.
We've been watching Edwin Reardon disintegrate under the pressure of his own artistic conscience.
Now let's turn to the man who thrives precisely by having none of those scruples: Jasper Milvain.
What's so unsettling about Milvain is that Gissing gives him all the best lines.
He's not a villain you can dismiss — he's articulate, funny, and almost always right about how the literary market actually works.
Listen to this from early in the novel, where he lays out his entire philosophy in one breath.

"My intuition is so strong that I can make a little experience go an immense way... I have the special faculty of an extempore writer. Never in my life shall I do anything of solid literary value; I shall always despise the people I write for. But my path will be that of success."
The audacity of it is breathtaking — he announces self-contempt for his own audience as a credential.
And structurally, Gissing places this confession so early because he wants us to have no excuse: we were warned from the beginning.
And historically, that self-knowledge is part of what makes Milvain so modern.
The 1880s saw an explosion of cheap periodicals, syndicates, and literary agents — the whole apparatus of commodified writing that we take for granted today.
Milvain simply names the mechanism that everyone else pretends doesn't exist.
He says it with almost clinical directness:
"I shall never write for writing's sake, only to make money. All my plans and efforts will have money in view — all. I shan't allow anything to come in the way of my material advancement."
The repetition of that word "all" — and then the blunt italic weight of it at the end — that's not boasting, that's a programme.
And a programme, unlike a principle, has no room for sentiment.
What gets me, re-reading this, is how much Jasper enjoys saying it.
There's a performance quality to his candour — he's not just being honest, he's being ostentatiously honest, almost as a form of vanity.
He even says so himself later on.

"Nearly all men who have their way to make think as I do, but most feel obliged to adopt a false tone, to talk about literary conscientiousness, and so on. I simply say what I think, with no pretences."
He's positioning his cynicism as a kind of integrity — which is a very neat trick.
And Gissing lets him have it, which I find both admirable and slightly maddening.
That tension you're describing, Caroline, is actually built into the prose style whenever Jasper speaks.
He has this wonderful passage where he's describing how to write newspaper leaders — what he calls padding inflated into eloquence.
He explains the technique with such relish that you can't tell whether he's mocking it or mastering it.
"You call a cigar a 'convoluted weed,' and so on, you know; that passes for facetiousness."
And then he says he's never actually tried that style yet — but he shouldn't wonder if he managed it brilliantly.
The comedy is in the gap between the contempt and the ambition — he despises the form even as he can't wait to colonise it.
And Whelpdale — Jasper's less glamorous counterpart — embodies exactly where that logic leads when it's followed to its conclusion.
His scheme for the magazine Chit-Chat is one of the funniest and most frightening passages in the book.
He describes his target readership with complete seriousness:

"People of this kind want something to occupy them in trains and on 'buses and trams. As a rule they care for no newspapers except the Sunday ones; what they want is the lightest and frothiest of chit-chatty information — bits of stories, bits of description, bits of scandal, bits of jokes, bits of statistics, bits of foolery."
That incantation of "bits" — six times in a single sentence — is Gissing's prose enacting the very fragmentation it's describing.
And of course the magazine is a commercial triumph, which is the darkest joke of all.
That detail about Whelpdale succeeding — it lands like a small, cold stone.
Because by that point in the novel we've watched Reardon destroyed for caring about his work.
And then there's this extraordinary moment in chapter thirty-seven where we see Jasper at the height of his powers.
Gissing describes him as looking five-and-thirty though only in his twenty-ninth year — the ambition has literally aged him.
But then there's this final, chilling detail about how he laughed.
"He laughed frequently, and with a throwing back of the head which seemed to express a spirit of triumph."
That gesture — the head thrown back — is the posture of a man who has won a war he declared on everyone around him.
It's a superb piece of physical characterisation — one gesture that tells you everything about where Jasper has arrived.
And what I find structurally fascinating is how Gissing distributes his desires across the novel.
In chapter twenty-four he gives Jasper this long, almost lyrical speech about what success actually means to him.
"My aim is to have easy command of all the pleasures desired by a cultivated man. I want to live among beautiful things, and never to be troubled by a thought of vulgar difficulties."
"I want to travel and enrich my mind in foreign countries. I want to associate on equal terms with refined and interesting people."
That repetition of "I want" is the engine of the whole character — not ideology, not art, just appetite, stated without apology.
The man is a pure product of his market, and Gissing makes him almost seductive as a result.
And yet, as Eleanor says, seductive — which I think is the really uncomfortable thing for the reader.
Because his programme works.
The market rewards exactly what Jasper offers it — facility, topicality, and total absence of inconvenient scruple.
Gissing published this novel in 1891, but his diagnosis of the attention economy — the bit-sized, the frothy, the quarter-educated audience — reads like a commentary written last week.
Which may be why the novel still stings rather than merely historical.
Jasper's triumph is built, of course, on choices — and not all of them purely professional ones.
When we come back, we'll look at someone caught between the worlds that Jasper moves through so easily: Marian Yule, whose position in this story is among the most painful Gissing ever created.
We've been tracing Jasper Milvain's calculated ascent through the literary marketplace — his willingness to treat writing as commerce and charm as currency.
Now I want to turn to the character whose fate throws Milvain's ambitions into sharpest relief: Marian Yule, and the particular kind of trap she finds herself in.
Marian is the character I return to most on re-reads, and I think it's because her trap is so precisely constructed.
She isn't simply poor, or simply unlucky in love — she is pinned from every direction.
There's a line that stops me every time I read it.
"She was not a woman, but a mere machine for reading and writing."
And then Gissing immediately asks, on her behalf: did her father never think of this?
She isn't raging at the world. She's asking whether she even registers as a person to the man who most shapes her life.
That line is so economical it almost hides how brutal it is.
Gissing gives us a legal or mechanical definition — a machine — and the shock is that it fits.
But what I find architecturally fascinating is how he extends that same logic into the Reading-room scenes.
He gothicizes the British Museum. He turns it into something genuinely sinister.
Listen to this passage — Marian's sitting under the dome as the fog thickens, and Gissing writes:
"The readers who sat here at these radiating lines of desks, what were they but hapless flies caught in a huge web, its nucleus the great circle of the Catalogue?"
The Catalogue — that great index of all recorded knowledge — becomes the spider at the centre of a trap.
The very instrument of enlightenment is recast as the mechanism of imprisonment.
The British Museum Reading-room in the 1880s was a genuine institution of aspiration — the place where self-educated men came to improve themselves.
And yet for someone in Marian's position, doing drudge-work for her father's projects, it's simply a workplace she cannot escape.
What Gissing captures — and what the fog does atmospherically — is the collapse of that aspirational promise.
The passage where she simply cannot force herself to work goes further than atmosphere, though.
She articulates a genuine intellectual critique of the literary marketplace.

"When already there was more good literature in the world than any mortal could cope with in his lifetime, here was she exhausting herself in the manufacture of printed stuff which no one even pretended to be more than a commodity for the day's market."
That word — manufacture — is doing real work.
It places literary production firmly inside the industrial economy, and Marian herself inside it as a unit of labour.
And she knows it. That's what makes it so bleak. There's no false consciousness here.
Gissing is quite explicit about this quality in Marian — her almost painful lucidity.

"Her candour was allied with clear insight into the possibilities of falsehood; she was not readily the victim of illusion; thinking much, and speaking little, she had not come to her twenty-third year without perceiving what a distance lay between a girl's dream of life as it might be and life as it is."
That pairing — life as it might be and life as it is — is almost a thesis statement for the whole novel.
And yet she does not speak it aloud. She internalises everything.
That silence is structural, not just psychological.
Gissing tells us she would be thought cynical if she spoke her thoughts. So she doesn't speak them.
Which means her most acute perceptions are locked inside the narration — available to us, invisible to every other character.
It's a kind of tragic irony built into the very free indirect style Gissing uses throughout.
And then there's the passage about literary rancour — where she watches her father and is simply horrified.
"Such things were enough to make all literature appear a morbid excrescence upon human life."
Excrescence. Not a malfunction or a failure — a growth. Something the body of human life would be healthier without.
It's a remarkable word to put in the mind of a character whose entire existence is organised around literature.
Gissing is doing something quite precise there — he's showing us how the literary world poisons even those who depend on it.
The father is consumed by rancour, and the daughter watches and is contaminated by proximity.
She recoils from what she's condemned to. But recoiling doesn't get you out.
And yet — and this is what I love about Gissing's portrait of her — she doesn't entirely give up.
There's a passage near the end of her chapter-length reverie that is almost unbearably tender.
"She could labour on in the valley of the shadow of books, for a ray of dazzling sunshine might at any moment strike into its musty gloom."
The valley of the shadow of books — reworking the Twenty-Third Psalm, but with the darkness coming from the very objects of her work.
And the hope she clings to is not ambition or escape. It's love. A single ray of sunshine.
Given what we know is coming, it's devastating.
What strikes me in everything you've described is how clearly Marian sees — and how completely that clarity fails to protect her.
The novel seems to suggest that lucidity without power is its own kind of prison.

After the break, we'll be turning to Gissing's own literary self-awareness — the ways the novel plays games with ideas of authorship and failure, and what it means when a novelist makes his failures so visible.
We've been dwelling on what it costs Marian to inhabit that in-between world — neither fully scholar nor fully free.
Now I want to turn to the writers themselves — Reardon, Biffen — and the ideas about fiction they carry into their poverty.
What strikes me first is that Gissing gives Biffen a fully worked-out literary manifesto — not a vague aspiration, but a genuine aesthetic programme.
And he states it with extraordinary precision.
Biffen calls his project, and I want to read this carefully:
"an absolute realism in the sphere of the ignobly decent."
That phrase — ignobly decent — is doing so much work.
It's not squalor, not tragedy, not even pathos — it's the specific dullness of people who are just about managing.
The class dimension here is absolutely central, and I think it gets underplayed.
Biffen is not talking about the Victorian working poor in the sense of Dickens's suffering masses.
He's talking about a stratum that had no dramatic profile at all — the clerks, the minor tradespeople, the failed professionals.
People whose lives didn't even qualify as interesting misery.
And Biffen names Zola and Dickens with real precision — Zola makes his vile figures heroic through dramatic scale, Dickens through comedy.
Both are essentially falsifications of that middle stratum's experience, however brilliant they are in other ways.
What I love is the moment Biffen becomes almost confessional about the outcome of his own programme.
He says he's going to reproduce this overheard love scene verbatim, without editorial comment.
"The result will be something unutterably tedious. Precisely. That is the stamp of the ignobly decent life."
He announces the tedium as a virtue — as the proof of truth.
There's something almost heroic and deeply absurd about it simultaneously.
And Gissing deepens the manifesto when Biffen goes further — into the anti-dramatic.
This is the passage I find genuinely radical, even now.
Biffen says:
"When the man and woman are to meet for a great scene of passion, let it all be frustrated by one or other of them having a bad cold in the head."
That is an attack on every novelistic convention simultaneously — the climactic scene, the beautiful heroine, the well-timed revelation.
And he insists it must be done seriously, coldly — not a hint of facetiousness, or the whole effect collapses into satire.
There's a painful irony lurking here that Gissing never lets us forget.
Biffen and Reardon hold these exacting, genuinely interesting ideas about fiction.
And they're surrounded by commercially successful writers who hold no ideas at all about fiction — or none they'd admit to.
Reardon articulates this with barely suppressed fury at one point.
"They have never known struggle; not they. They are public-school men, University men, club men, society men."
The repetition — men, men, men — is almost a chant of class resentment.
And it's true — the literary market of the 1880s was substantially underwritten by readers who shared exactly that background.
What breaks my heart slightly is what Gissing tells us about Reardon's relationship to his own reviews.
He avoids them — not out of arrogance, but because he already knows exactly what they'll say, and he knows they'll be wrong.
Gissing puts it with such quiet precision:
"commendation was pleasant, but it so often aimed amiss, and censure was for the most part so unintelligent."
It's not bitterness, exactly — it's a kind of exhausted clarity.
He's trapped between the market's incomprehension and his own exacting standards.
And Gissing is honest — sometimes uncomfortably so — about why Reardon fails on his own terms too.
There's a devastating passage early in the novel about his temperament.
"He was the kind of man who cannot struggle against adverse conditions, but whom prosperity warms to the exercise of his powers."
Gissing is not excusing him — he's diagnosing him.
The irony is that the very sensitivity that makes Reardon a potentially fine writer makes him constitutionally unfit for the conditions under which he must write.
The market doesn't just defeat him financially — it defeats him psychologically, structurally, before he even puts pen to paper.
That diagnosis has a social dimension that I'd press a little harder.
Reardon's ideal conditions — a legacy, leisure, no domestic pressure — are precisely the conditions those public-school men he resents were born into.
He needs what they have by birthright.
And the brief window when he does have a legacy — he writes essays, lets himself rest, finds his footing.
The novel is showing us that poverty isn't just an inconvenience for an artist of Reardon's type — it is a categorical disqualification.
And yet Biffen persists — cheerfully, almost serenely — in a garret, with almost nothing.
His poverty seems if anything to clarify his purpose rather than corrode it.
Which is perhaps Gissing's most tender joke — the man with the most impractical literary theory is the most practically committed to it.
So we have two men holding literature to the highest possible standard — and being destroyed, in different ways and at different speeds, for doing so.
Which makes the novel's comic register all the more striking — because there is genuine comedy here, and it cuts in some surprising directions.
We've been exploring how Gissing plays with narrative form and the spectacle of literary failure.
But there's another register running through this novel — a sharp, almost gleeful comedy — and that's what we want to open up now.
What strikes me every time I re-read this novel is how genuinely funny Gissing can be — and how underacknowledged that is.
There's a passage in Chapter Five where Reardon is trying to discuss Tibullus — the Roman elegist — with someone who clearly has no patience for that sort of thing.
The response he gets is just this wonderful deflation.
'Oh, dear! Oh, dear! — Forgive me, Mr Reardon; my feelings were too much for me; those names have been my horror ever since I was a schoolboy.'
And then the pivot — delivered with such airy reasonableness — that classical scholarship is 'indifferently paid and in very small demand.'
It's the market speaking directly to the idealist, and Gissing times it perfectly.
That timing is everything, isn't it — the structure of the joke is really a structural argument about the novel's whole world.
Gissing gives us the naïve question — Reardon talking about Tibullus with genuine enthusiasm — and then the market just flattens it.
It's not cruel comedy — it's comedy that reveals a systemic truth.
And then notice: 'It hasn't occurred to you to try your hand at fiction?' — said as if fiction were simply the sensible alternative.
The whole literary economy of the novel is compressed into that one polite suggestion.
What Gissing captures there is historically precise, not just satirical.
Classical scholarship in the 1880s really was a poor living outside of a university fellowship — which most men of Reardon's background couldn't obtain.
So that conversational dismissal — 'indifferently paid and in very small demand' — is not a joke at Reardon's expense so much as a cold reading of the actual market conditions.
The comedy and the economic reality are the same thing.
Gissing doesn't have to exaggerate for satirical effect — the situation is already absurd enough.
And the comedy deepens later when Reardon himself turns the same unsentimental eye on his own situation — but with a kind of rueful delight.
There's that extraordinary exchange between Reardon and Biffen in Chapter Twenty-Seven, where they've been ground down by poverty and isolation — and yet Reardon suddenly sounds almost cheerful.
He says, with perfect seriousness:
'Doesn't it strike you that you and I are very respectable persons? We really have no vices.'
And then he goes on — why haven't they become drunkards, revolutionists, haranguing in Regent's Park?
Their poverty hasn't made them dangerous — just quietly, impeccably virtuous — and Reardon finds that almost comical.
That passage is doing something very precise with point of view — Reardon is both inside the joke and the subject of it.
He's laughing at the gap between his circumstances and the moral respectability those circumstances haven't actually eroded.
And there's something almost tragic underneath it — the question 'why don't we run amuck against law and order?' is genuinely plaintive if you listen to it right.
These men have every reason to be angry and they've somehow remained merely — polite.
It's very bitter, but it's also very funny — and holding both things at once is one of Gissing's real gifts.
The phrase 'shining lights of morality' — placed on a social pedestal — is worth pausing on.
Victorian respectability was intimately connected to social position — you were moral because you had the means and the leisure to appear so.
Reardon's joke inverts that entirely: here are two men with no social pedestal at all, and they remain stubbornly, absurdly virtuous.
It quietly demolishes the Victorian moral economy — the idea that virtue flows downward from prosperity.
Which brings us to Jasper Milvain — the novel's great performer of cheerfulness — who handles emotional difficulty in a very different way.
There's a wonderful small moment in Chapter Thirty, where Jasper and Marian are together before what is clearly going to be a painful conversation.
The narrator tells us, with magnificent dryness:
'It was as necessary to him as to her to have a respite before the graver discussion began.'

And then — 'He seized gladly the opportunity she offered, and read several pages of manuscript, slipping from one topic to another. To hear him one would have supposed that he was in his ordinary mood; he laughed at his own jokes and points.'
That 'laughed at his own jokes and points' — it's devastating in its precision.
Jasper isn't deceiving Marian — he's performing for himself, keeping the machinery of his confidence running.
That's the comedy of self-management, isn't it — and it's quite different from Reardon's comedy.
Reardon laughs at his situation from the outside, with a kind of philosophical distance.
Jasper laughs to keep himself functional — it's a professional technique as much as anything else.
The narrator's phrase 'to hear him one would have supposed' is doing the ironic work — it tells us there is a gap between performance and interior state.
And Gissing leaves it there — doesn't moralize, doesn't explain — just marks the gap and moves on.
There's a real cost to that performance, though — and I think the novel is quite clear-eyed about it.
Jasper has cultivated cheerfulness as a social instrument so thoroughly that by this point we can't quite tell where the instrument ends and the person begins.
In that sense his comedy is the opposite of Reardon's — it doesn't reveal anything true; it conceals.
And the fact that both modes — transparency and concealment — are rendered with the same dry precision says something about Gissing's moral evenhandedness.
He doesn't prefer Reardon's honesty to Jasper's management — he just shows us both, exactly.
Comedy as revelation, comedy as concealment — and always, underneath both, this question of what a literary life actually costs the people living it.
That question of cost — whether literature ultimately offers anything worth the sacrifice — is exactly where we want to end, and it's where we're heading next.

segments.title: Closing: New Grub Street's Enduring Question

utterances.text: We've been laughing — sometimes uncomfortably — at the comedy of literary ambition.
But Gissing never lets the laughter last long before something darker moves in underneath it.
What I want to end with is the question the novel ultimately forces on us: what does this world cost the people trapped inside it?
That question is where the novel becomes genuinely devastating, I think.
Because Gissing constructs the whole book around this grinding erosion — of hope, of identity, of the very language a writer uses to understand himself.
There's a moment with Reardon that I find almost unbearable to read, precisely because of how quietly it's delivered.
"Let the man of letters be forgotten; he was seeking for remunerative employment, just as if he had never written a line."
That phrase — 'just as if he had never written a line' — is annihilation dressed as practicality.
Reardon isn't being defeated by an enemy; he's erasing himself, and Gissing makes it sound almost reasonable.
That gap between the horror of the act and the calm of the prose — that's where Gissing's art lives.
Eleanor's right that the prose stays calm — but I think that calmness is also a social indictment.
Gissing understood that poverty doesn't announce itself with melodrama; it seeps in, accumulates in small details, and becomes the texture of a life.
There's a passage about Reardon's clothes — and what strikes me is that the degradation has become almost self-administered by the time we get there.
"These seedy habiliments were the token of his degradation, and at times he regarded them — happening to see himself in a shop mirror — with pleasurable contempt."
'Pleasurable contempt.' That's an extraordinary formulation.
He's internalized the judgment of the market, and now he uses it as a kind of perverse self-flagellation.
What Gissing is showing us is a man who has been so thoroughly processed by an economic system that he does its work for it.
And it isn't only Reardon.
Marian Yule is equally destroyed by this world, and Gissing finds an image for her suffering that I've never been able to shake.
It's the fog passage — this London fog that isn't just weather but something almost theological.
"The thick black fog penetrated every corner of the house. It could be smelt and tasted."
"Such an atmosphere produces low-spirited languor even in the vigorous and hopeful; to those wasted by suffering it is the very reek of the bottomless pit, poisoning the soul."
'The very reek of the bottomless pit.' Gissing doesn't say that metaphorically; he means it almost literally.
This is a hellish world — the fog is its atmosphere, its ambient condition.
And Marian lies in it, not sleeping, not awake — suspended in suffering the novel treats as almost too acute for language.
What Caroline's put her finger on is something I keep coming back to with Gissing — the way he makes suffering environmental.
It isn't individual failure; it's atmospheric pressure.
The system isn't a villain you can identify and oppose — it's the very air these characters breathe.
And that, I think, is why the novel still feels so modern — the conditions have changed, but the logic hasn't.
The logic of the market eating its own creative workers — no, that hasn't changed in the slightest.
What Gissing understood — and what makes this more than a period piece — is that the market doesn't need to be malevolent; it just needs to be indifferent.
Reardon's books weren't actively destroyed; they simply stopped being commercially viable.
And the system shrugged, and moved on, and Reardon was left to erase himself.
I want to say something about why I keep returning to this novel, personally.
It's not comfortable reading — it refuses the consolations of irony, refuses to let you feel cleverer than the characters.
Gissing actually wants you to feel the weight of what these people are carrying.
And I think that demand on the reader — that refusal to make it easy — is part of what makes it a great novel.
I think that's the right note on which to end.
New Grub Street is a novel that refuses to console — about writing, about poverty, about what a market economy does to the people who care most about things it can't price.
We've moved today from the structures of ambition and failure, through the comedy of literary pretension, and arrived here — at the human cost beneath it all.
My warmest thanks to Eleanor Hartley, James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt — this has been a conversation I'll be thinking about for a long time.
And to you, our listeners — thank you for spending this time with Gissing, and with us.

c1:p100.text:
‘I maintain that we people of brains are justified in supplying the mob
      with the food it likes. We are not geniuses, and if we sit down in a
      spirit of long-eared gravity we shall produce only commonplace stuff. Let
      us use our wits to earn money, and make the best we can of our lives. If
      only I had the skill, I would produce novels out-trashing the trashiest
      that ever sold fifty thousand copies. But it needs skill, mind you: and to
      deny it is a gross error of the literary pedants. To please the vulgar you
      must, one way or another, incarnate the genius of vulgarity. For my own
      part, I shan’t be able to address the bulkiest multitude; my talent
      doesn’t lend itself to that form. I shall write for the upper middle-class
      of intellect, the people who like to feel that what they are reading has
      some special cleverness, but who can’t distinguish between stones and
      paste. That’s why I’m so slow in warming to the work. Every month I feel
      surer of myself, however.
c1:p100.summary: Jasper argues that people of talent should supply the mob's preferred fare, not sit in solemn gravity producing commonplace work. He emphasises that skill is required to create commercially successful trash. He will not address the mass market; instead he targets the upper-middle-class intelligentsia who desire clever work. He notes his monthly growing confidence and cites his recent West End piece as proof of his ability to hit the mark.
c1:p100.best_quote: To please the vulgar you must, one way or another, incarnate the genius of vulgarity.

c15:p93.text:
‘Darling, they do struggle. But it’s as if an ever-increasing weight were
      round their necks; it drags them lower and lower. The world has no pity on
      a man who can’t do or produce something it thinks worth money. You may be
      a divine poet, and if some good fellow doesn’t take pity on you you will
      starve by the roadside. Society is as blind and brutal as fate. I have no
      right to complain of my own ill-fortune; it’s my own fault (in a sense)
      that I can’t continue as well as I began; if I could write books as good
      as the early ones I should earn money. For all that, it’s hard that I must
      be kicked aside as worthless just because I don’t know a trade.’
c15:p93.summary: Reardon argues that despite the efforts of struggling men with families, an ever-increasing burden drags them down; society is indifferent to human worth and offers no mercy to those without marketable skills; he accepts some personal responsibility but indicts the system as cruel and blind.
c15:p93.best_quote: The world has no pity on a man who can't do or produce something it thinks worth money. You may be a divine poet, and if some good fellow doesn't take pity on you you will starve by the roadside. Society is as blind and brutal as fate.

c31:p1.text:
But try to imagine a personality wholly unfitted for the rough and tumble
      of the world’s labour-market. From the familiar point of view these men
      were worthless; view them in possible relation to a humane order of
      Society, and they are admirable citizens. Nothing is easier than to
      condemn a type of character which is unequal to the coarse demands of life
      as it suits the average man. These two were richly endowed with the kindly
      and the imaginative virtues; if fate threw them amid incongruous
      circumstances, is their endowment of less value? You scorn their
      passivity; but it was their nature and their merit to be passive.
c31:p1.summary: The narrator defends Reardon and Biffen as admirable in a humane society, arguing their passivity is a merit rather than a failing.
c31:p1.best_quote: These two were richly endowed with the kindly and the imaginative virtues; if fate threw them amid incongruous circumstances, is their endowment of less value?

c6:p93.text:
‘That half-year abroad, and the extraordinary shock of happiness which
      followed at once upon it, have disturbed the balance of my nature. It was
      adjusted to circumstances of hardship, privation, struggle. A temperament
      like mine can’t pass through such a violent change of conditions without
      being greatly affected; I have never since been the man I was before I
      left England. The stage I had then reached was the result of a slow and
      elaborate building up; I could look back and see the processes by which I
      had grown from the boy who was a mere bookworm to the man who had all but
      succeeded as a novelist. It was a perfectly natural, sober development.
      But in the last two years and a half I can distinguish no order. In living
      through it, I have imagined from time to time that my powers were coming
      to their ripest; but that was mere delusion. Intellectually, I have fallen
      back. The probability is that this wouldn’t matter, if only I could live
      on in peace of mind; I should recover my equilibrium, and perhaps once
      more understand myself. But the due course of things is troubled by my
      poverty.’
c6:p93.summary: Reardon analyzes how his sojourn abroad and the subsequent shock of happiness with Amy disrupted his previously balanced development, leading to intellectual decline and mental paralysis aggravated by financial desperation; he contrasts his formerly natural development with his current disordered state.
c6:p93.best_quote: A temperament like mine can't pass through such a violent change of conditions without being greatly affected; I have never since been the man I was before I left England... I have imagined from time to time that my powers were coming to their ripest; but that was mere delusion. Intellectually, I have fallen back... But the due course of things is troubled by my poverty.

c15:p0.text:
The past twelve months had added several years to Edwin Reardon’s seeming
      age; at thirty-three he would generally have been taken for forty. His
      bearing, his personal habits, were no longer those of a young man; he
      walked with a stoop and pressed noticeably on the stick he carried; it was
      rare for him to show the countenance which tells of present cheerfulness
      or glad onward-looking; there was no spring in his step; his voice had
      fallen to a lower key, and often he spoke with that hesitation in choice
      of words which may be noticed in persons whom defeat has made
      self-distrustful. Ceaseless perplexity and dread gave a wandering,
      sometimes a wild, expression to his eyes.
c15:p0.summary: Reardon has aged dramatically in the past year, his body and bearing showing the ravages of mental strain and deprivation; he moves with difficulty, sleeps poorly, and his eyes show wild distress.
c15:p0.best_quote: at thirty-three he would generally have been taken for forty

c9:p13.text:
Sometimes the three hours’ labour of a morning resulted in half-a-dozen
      lines, corrected into illegibility. His brain would not work; he could not
      recall the simplest synonyms; intolerable faults of composition drove him
      mad. He would write a sentence beginning thus: ‘She took a book with a
      look of—;’ or thus: ‘A revision of this decision would have made him
      an object of derision.’ Or, if the period were otherwise inoffensive, it
      ran in a rhythmic gallop which was torment to the ear. All this, in spite
      of the fact that his former books had been noticeably good in style. He
      had an appreciation of shapely prose which made him scorn himself for the
      kind of stuff he was now turning out. ‘I can’t help it; it must go; the
      time is passing.’
c9:p13.summary: On bad mornings, Reardon produces only half-a-dozen lines of illegible corrections; his brain fails him, syntax collapses into awkward repetitions ('She took a book with a look of—'), yet he forces himself to continue for time's sake.
c9:p13.best_quote: 'I can't help it; it must go; the time is passing.'

c4:p84.text:
‘And yet,’ he continued, ‘of course it isn’t only for the sake of
      reputation that one tries to do uncommon work. There’s the shrinking from
      conscious insincerity of workmanship—which most of the writers
      nowadays seem never to feel. “It’s good enough for the market”; that
      satisfies them. And perhaps they are justified.
c4:p84.summary: Edwin continues his meditation: he cannot rule his life by absolute ideals; everything is relative. Yet he cannot help but try to make his work good, even knowing it can't be first-rate—a contradiction he acknowledges.
c4:p84.best_quote: There's the shrinking from conscious insincerity of workmanship—which most of the writers nowadays seem never to feel.

c12:p1.text:
Between him and her there was no longer perfect confidence. Her silence
      meant reproach, and—whatever might have been the case before—there
      was no doubt that she now discussed him with her mother, possibly with
      other people. It was not likely that she concealed his own opinion of the
      book he had just finished; all their acquaintances would be prepared to
      greet its publication with private scoffing or with mournful shaking of
      the head. His feeling towards Amy entered upon a new phase. The stability
      of his love was a source of pain; condemning himself, he felt at the same
      time that he was wronged. A coldness which was far from representing the
      truth began to affect his manner and speech, and Amy did not seem to
      notice it, at all events she made no kind of protest. They no longer
      talked of the old subjects, but of those mean concerns of material life
      which formerly they had agreed to dismiss as quickly as possible. Their
      relations to each other—not long ago an inexhaustible topic—would
      not bear spoken comment; both were too conscious of the danger-signal when
      they looked that way.
c12:p1.summary: The novel traces how Amy's silence and discussions with her mother have broken Reardon's confidence in their marriage; they have shifted from discussing intimate matters to mere practical concerns of survival.
c12:p1.best_quote: Their relations to each other—not long ago an inexhaustible topic—would not bear spoken comment; both were too conscious of the danger-signal when they looked that way.

c31:p89.text:
‘To have had even a small reputation, and to have outlived it, is a sort
      of anticipation of death. The man Edwin Reardon, whose name was sometimes
      spoken in a tone of interest, is really and actually dead. And what
      remains of me is resigned to that. I have an odd fancy that it will make
      death itself easier; it is as if only half of me had now to die.’
c31:p89.summary: Reardon philosophizes that outliving his reputation is a kind of death; he feels the person he was is already dead.
c31:p89.best_quote: To have had even a small reputation, and to have outlived it, is a sort of anticipation of death. The man Edwin Reardon, whose name was sometimes spoken in a tone of interest, is really and actually dead. And what remains of me is resigned to that. I have an odd fancy that it will make death itself easier; it is as if only half of me had now to die.

c6:p63.text:
‘’Tis my vocation, Hal! You might think I hadn’t experience enough, to
      begin with. But my intuition is so strong that I can make a little
      experience go an immense way. Most people would imagine I had been wasting
      my time these last few years, just sauntering about, reading nothing but
      periodicals, making acquaintance with loafers of every description. The
      truth is, I have been collecting ideas, and ideas that are convertible
      into coin of the realm, my boy; I have the special faculty of an extempore
      writer. Never in my life shall I do anything of solid literary value; I
      shall always despise the people I write for. But my path will be that of
      success. I have always said it, and now I’m sure of it.’
c6:p63.summary: Jasper defends his unconventional path to success, claiming that despite appearing to waste time, he has been collecting convertible ideas and has a special faculty for extempore writing. He frankly admits he will never produce solid literature and will despise his audience, but insists success is assured.
c6:p63.best_quote: My intuition is so strong that I can make a little experience go an immense way... I have the special faculty of an extempore writer. Never in my life shall I do anything of solid literary value; I shall always despise the people I write for. But my path will be that of success.

c8:p180.text:
‘I like to hear people say that, but it’ll mean savage work. When we were
      all at Finden last year, I told the girls that it would be another twelve
      months before I could support myself. Now I am forced to do it. And I
      don’t like work; my nature is lazy. I shall never write for writing’s
      sake, only to make money. All my plans and efforts will have money in view—all.
      I shan’t allow anything to come in the way of my material advancement.’
c8:p180.summary: Jasper bluntly states he will not write for its own sake, that all his efforts serve material advancement, and that he lacks the natural inclination toward work.
c8:p180.best_quote: I shan't allow anything to come in the way of my material advancement.

c24:p54.text:
‘That’s precisely the truth. Nearly all men who have their way to make
      think as I do, but most feel obliged to adopt a false tone, to talk about
      literary conscientiousness, and so on. I simply say what I think, with no
      pretences. I should like to be conscientious, but it’s a luxury I can’t
      afford. I’ve told you all this often enough, you know.’
c24:p54.summary: Jasper argues that most aspiring writers share his pragmatic views but hide them; he alone speaks honestly about the necessity of worldly ambition.
c24:p54.best_quote: Nearly all men who have their way to make think as I do, but most feel obliged to adopt a false tone, to talk about literary conscientiousness, and so on. I simply say what I think, with no pretences. I should like to be conscientious, but it's a luxury I can't afford.

c14:p76.text:
‘By no means. That’s not my line. The kind of thing in which one makes a
      column out of what would fill six lines of respectable prose. You call a
      cigar a “convoluted weed,” and so on, you know; that passes for
      facetiousness. I’ve never really tried my hand at that style yet; I
      shouldn’t wonder if I managed it brilliantly. Some day I’ll write a few
      exercises; just take two lines of some good prose writer, and expand them
      into twenty, in half-a-dozen different ways. Excellent mental gymnastics!’
c14:p76.summary: Jasper explains the style of newspaper leaders: inflating trivial ideas into elaborate prose through verbal pyrotechnics, which he suggests he could master easily.
c14:p76.best_quote: You call a cigar a "convoluted weed," and so on, you know; that passes for facetiousness.

c33:p49.text:
‘No, I am perfectly serious. Let me explain my principle. I would have the
      paper address itself to the quarter-educated; that is to say, the great
      new generation that is being turned out by the Board schools, the young
      men and women who can just read, but are incapable of sustained attention.
      People of this kind want something to occupy them in trains and on ‘buses
      and trams. As a rule they care for no newspapers except the Sunday ones;
      what they want is the lightest and frothiest of chit-chatty information—bits
      of stories, bits of description, bits of scandal, bits of jokes, bits of
      statistics, bits of foolery. Am I not right? Everything must be very
      short, two inches at the utmost; their attention can’t sustain itself
      beyond two inches. Even chat is too solid for them: they want chit-chat.’
c33:p49.summary: Whelpdale explains his philosophy: the magazine should target the quarter-educated mass produced by Board schools—young people who can barely read and cannot sustain attention. They want brief fragments of information while travelling, not substantial articles. Everything must be extremely short, as their concentration cannot exceed two inches of text.
c33:p49.best_quote: People of this kind want something to occupy them in trains and on 'buses and trams. As a rule they care for no newspapers except the Sunday ones; what they want is the lightest and frothiest of chit-chatty information—bits of stories, bits of description, bits of scandal, bits of jokes, bits of statistics, bits of foolery.

c37:p61.text:
Jasper had changed considerably in appearance since that last holiday that
      he spent in his mother’s house at Finden. At present he would have been
      taken for five-and-thirty, though only in his twenty-ninth year; his hair
      was noticeably thinning; his moustache had grown heavier; a wrinkle or two
      showed beneath his eyes; his voice was softer, yet firmer. It goes without
      saying that his evening uniform lacked no point of perfection, and somehow
      it suggested a more elaborate care than that of other men in the room. He
      laughed frequently, and with a throwing back of the head which seemed to
      express a spirit of triumph.
c37:p61.summary: Jasper has aged considerably and appears ten years older than his twenty-nine years; his manner and dress suggest meticulous care and a spirit of triumph.

c24:p108.text:
‘Yes, I will tell you. My aim is to have easy command of all the pleasures
      desired by a cultivated man. I want to live among beautiful things, and
      never to be troubled by a thought of vulgar difficulties. I want to travel
      and enrich my mind in foreign countries. I want to associate on equal
      terms with refined and interesting people. I want to be known, to be
      familiarly referred to, to feel when I enter a room that people regard me
      with some curiosity.’
c24:p108.summary: Jasper defines success as commanding cultivated pleasures: living beautifully, traveling, associating with refined people, and gaining social recognition and curiosity.
c24:p108.best_quote: My aim is to have easy command of all the pleasures desired by a cultivated man. I want to live among beautiful things, and never to be troubled by a thought of vulgar difficulties. I want to travel and enrich my mind in foreign countries. I want to associate on equal terms with refined and interesting people. I want to be known, to be familiarly referred to, to feel when I enter a room that people regard me with some curiosity.

c8:p11.text:
She went up to her room, and wept over the wretchedness of all their
      lives. Her loneliness had seemed harder to bear than ever since that last
      holiday. For a moment, in the lanes about Finden, there had come to her a
      vision of joy such as fate owed her youth; but it had faded, and she could
      no longer hope for its return. She was not a woman, but a mere machine for
      reading and writing. Did her father never think of this? He was not the
      only one to suffer from the circumstances in which poverty had involved
      him.
c8:p11.summary: In her room, Marian weeps over the misery of her family's circumstances, recalling her brief moment of happiness at Finden and mourning her lost opportunity for love.
c8:p11.best_quote: She was not a woman, but a mere machine for reading and writing.

c8:p19.text:
The fog grew thicker; she looked up at the windows beneath the dome and
      saw that they were a dusky yellow. Then her eye discerned an official
      walking along the upper gallery, and in pursuance of her grotesque humour,
      her mocking misery, she likened him to a black, lost soul, doomed to
      wander in an eternity of vain research along endless shelves. Or again,
      the readers who sat here at these radiating lines of desks, what were they
      but hapless flies caught in a huge web, its nucleus the great circle of
      the Catalogue? Darker, darker. From the towering wall of volumes seemed to
      emanate visible motes, intensifying the obscurity; in a moment the
      book-lined circumference of the room would be but a featureless
      prison-limit.
c8:p19.summary: As fog darkens the Reading-room, Marian's despair manifests in gothicized perception: the library becomes a prison, its inhabitants doomed souls or trapped flies.
c8:p19.best_quote: Or again, the readers who sat here at these radiating lines of desks, what were they but hapless flies caught in a huge web, its nucleus the great circle of the Catalogue?

c8:p15.text:
One day at the end of the month she sat with books open before her, but by
      no effort could fix her attention upon them. It was gloomy, and one could
      scarcely see to read; a taste of fog grew perceptible in the warm,
      headachy air. Such profound discouragement possessed her that she could
      not even maintain the pretence of study; heedless whether anyone observed
      her, she let her hands fall and her head droop. She kept asking herself
      what was the use and purpose of such a life as she was condemned to lead.
      When already there was more good literature in the world than any mortal
      could cope with in his lifetime, here was she exhausting herself in the
      manufacture of printed stuff which no one even pretended to be more than a
      commodity for the day’s market. What unspeakable folly! To write—was
      not that the joy and the privilege of one who had an urgent message for
      the world?
c8:p15.summary: In the Museum on a gloomy day, Marian's concentration collapses as she questions the purpose of manufacturing literature for market consumption when the world already contains more books than anyone can read.
c8:p15.best_quote: What unspeakable folly! To write—was not that the joy and the privilege of one who had an urgent message for the world?

c14:p147.text:
Marian often went thus far in her speculation. Her candour was allied with
      clear insight into the possibilities of falsehood; she was not readily the
      victim of illusion; thinking much, and speaking little, she had not come
      to her twenty-third year without perceiving what a distance lay between a
      girl’s dream of life as it might be and life as it is. Had she invariably
      disclosed her thoughts, she would have earned the repute of a very
      sceptical and slightly cynical person.
c14:p147.summary: Marian's character is defined by candid perception of human hypocrisy and the gap between ideals and reality; she would be regarded as cynical if she spoke her thoughts aloud.
c14:p147.best_quote: Her candour was allied with clear insight into the possibilities of falsehood; she was not readily the victim of illusion; thinking much, and speaking little, she had not come to her twenty-third year without perceiving what a distance lay between a girl's dream of life as it might be and life as it is.

c13:p52.text:
It was the hateful spirit of literary rancour that ruled him; the spirit
      that made people eager to believe all evil, that blinded and maddened.
      Never had she felt so strongly the unworthiness of the existence to which
      she was condemned. That contemptible review, and now her father’s ignoble
      passion—such things were enough to make all literature appear a
      morbid excrescence upon human life.
c13:p52.summary: Marian condemns the hateful spirit of literary rancor that blinds and maddens, recognizing it in her father and recoiling from the contemptible existence to which she is condemned.
c13:p52.best_quote: such things were enough to make all literature appear a morbid excrescence upon human life

c14:p157.text:
The unhoped was all but granted her. She could labour on in the valley of
      the shadow of books, for a ray of dazzling sunshine might at any moment
      strike into its musty gloom.
c14:p157.summary: Marian concludes her reflections with hope: she can endure her dreary library work because love promises to illuminate her darkness.
c14:p157.best_quote: She could labour on in the valley of the shadow of books, for a ray of dazzling sunshine might at any moment strike into its musty gloom.

c10:p119.text:
‘I have thought of a new way of putting it. What I really aim at is an
      absolute realism in the sphere of the ignobly decent. The field, as I
      understand it, is a new one; I don’t know any writer who has treated
      ordinary vulgar life with fidelity and seriousness. Zola writes deliberate
      tragedies; his vilest figures become heroic from the place they fill in a
      strongly imagined drama. I want to deal with the essentially unheroic,
      with the day-to-day life of that vast majority of people who are at the
      mercy of paltry circumstance. Dickens understood the possibility of such
      work, but his tendency to melodrama on the one hand, and his humour on the
      other, prevented him from thinking of it. An instance, now. As I came
      along by Regent’s Park half an hour ago a man and a girl were walking
      close in front of me, love-making; I passed them slowly and heard a good
      deal of their talk—it was part of the situation that they should pay
      no heed to a stranger’s proximity. Now, such a love-scene as that has
      absolutely never been written down; it was entirely decent, yet vulgar to
      the nth power. Dickens would have made it ludicrous—a gross
      injustice. Other men who deal with low-class life would perhaps have
      preferred idealising it—an absurdity. For my own part, I am going to
      reproduce it verbatim, without one single impertinent suggestion of any
      point of view save that of honest reporting. The result will be something
      unutterably tedious. Precisely. That is the stamp of the ignobly decent
      life. If it were anything but tedious it would be untrue. I speak, of
      course, of its effect upon the ordinary reader.’
c10:p119.summary: Biffen expounds his theory of absolute realism applied to ordinary, vulgar life—rejecting both Zola's melodrama and Dickens's humor, insisting instead on verbatim reproduction of the tedious, unheroic reality of common people.
c10:p119.best_quote: I want to deal with the essentially unheroic, with the day-to-day life of that vast majority of people who are at the mercy of paltry circumstance

c10:p137.text:
‘It is worked out. We must have a rest from it. You, now—the best
      things you have done are altogether in conflict with novelistic
      conventionalities. It was because that blackguard review of “On Neutral
      Ground” clumsily hinted this that I first thought of you with interest.
      No, no; let us copy life. When the man and woman are to meet for a great
      scene of passion, let it all be frustrated by one or other of them having
      a bad cold in the head, and so on. Let the pretty girl get a disfiguring
      pimple on her nose just before the ball at which she is going to shine.
      Show the numberless repulsive features of common decent life. Seriously,
      coldly; not a hint of facetiousness, or the thing becomes different.’
c10:p137.summary: Biffen argues that realist fiction should reject dramatic convention in favor of mundane reality: love scenes interrupted by illness, beauty spoiled by pimples.
c10:p137.best_quote: When the man and woman are to meet for a great scene of passion, let it all be frustrated by one or other of them having a bad cold in the head

c27:p105.text:
‘With what magnificent scorn they would turn from us and our squalid
      feast! They have never known struggle; not they. They are public-school
      men, University men, club men, society men. An income of less than three
      or four hundred a year is inconceivable to them; that seems the minimum
      for an educated man’s support. It would be small-minded to think of them
      with rancour, but, by Apollo! I know that we should change places with
      them if the work we have done were justly weighed against theirs.’
c27:p105.summary: Reardon condemns the successful novelists as public-school men incapable of understanding poverty; he insists their literary work is inferior to his own but serves the market demand, and asserts that if true merit were weighed, he and Biffen would triumph.
c27:p105.best_quote: They have never known struggle; not they. They are public-school men, University men, club men, society men.

c16:p0.text:
One of Reardon’s minor worries at this time was the fear that by chance he
      might come upon a review of ‘Margaret Home.’ Since the publication of his
      first book he had avoided as far as possible all knowledge of what the
      critics had to say about him; his nervous temperament could not bear the
      agitation of reading these remarks, which, however inept, define an author
      and his work to so many people incapable of judging for themselves. No man
      or woman could tell him anything in the way of praise or blame which he
      did not already know quite well; commendation was pleasant, but it so
      often aimed amiss, and censure was for the most part so unintelligent. In
      the case of this latest novel he dreaded the sight of a review as he would
      have done a gash from a rusty knife. The judgments could not but be
      damnatory, and their expression in journalistic phrase would disturb his
      mind with evil rancour. No one would have insight enough to appreciate the
      nature and cause of his book’s demerits; every comment would be wide of
      the mark; sneer, ridicule, trite objection, would but madden him with a
      sense of injustice.
c16:p0.summary: Reardon dreads reading reviews of his latest novel 'Margaret Home,' fearing they will be unintelligent and wounding, unable to address the true causes of the book's failure.
c16:p0.best_quote: commendation was pleasant, but it so often aimed amiss, and censure was for the most part so unintelligent

c5:p34.text:
He was the kind of man who cannot struggle against adverse conditions, but
      whom prosperity warms to the exercise of his powers. Anything like the
      cares of responsibility would sooner or later harass him into
      unproductiveness. That he should produce much was in any case out of the
      question; possibly a book every two or three years might not prove too
      great a strain upon his delicate mental organism, but for him to attempt
      more than that would certainly be fatal to the peculiar merit of his work.
      Of this he was dimly conscious, and, on receiving his legacy, he put aside
      for nearly twelve months the new novel he had begun. To give his mind a
      rest he wrote several essays, much maturer than those which had formerly
      failed to find acceptance, and two of these appeared in magazines.
c5:p34.summary: Reardon is psychologically dependent on ease and cannot produce much without damaging his artistic integrity; he rests and writes essays before resuming novel-writing.
c5:p34.best_quote: He was the kind of man who cannot struggle against adverse conditions, but whom prosperity warms to the exercise of his powers.

c5:p13.text:
‘Oh, dear! Oh, dear!—Forgive me, Mr Reardon; my feelings were too
      much for me; those names have been my horror ever since I was a schoolboy.
      Far be it from me to discourage you, if your line is to be solid literary
      criticism; I will only mention, as a matter of fact, that such work is
      indifferently paid and in very small demand. It hasn’t occurred to you to
      try your hand at fiction?’
c5:p13.summary: The novelist reacts with exasperation to Tibullus, dismisses classical scholarship as indifferently paid and in small demand, and recommends fiction instead.

c27:p14.text:
‘Well,’ said Reardon, musing cheerfully, ‘I shall never become a drunkard;
      I haven’t that diathesis, to use your expression. Doesn’t it strike you
      that you and I are very respectable persons? We really have no vices. Put
      us on a social pedestal, and we should be shining lights of morality. I
      sometimes wonder at our inoffensiveness. Why don’t we run amuck against
      law and order? Why, at the least, don’t we become savage revolutionists,
      and harangue in Regent’s Park of a Sunday?’
c27:p14.summary: Reardon ironically praises his and Biffen's moral inoffensiveness, questioning why they haven't become revolutionaries or criminals given their poverty.
c27:p14.best_quote: Doesn't it strike you that you and I are very respectable persons? We really have no vices.

c30:p29.text:
It was as necessary to him as to her to have a respite before the graver
      discussion began. He seized gladly the opportunity she offered, and read
      several pages of manuscript, slipping from one topic to another. To hear
      him one would have supposed that he was in his ordinary mood; he laughed
      at his own jokes and points.
c30:p29.summary: The narrator observes that both Jasper and Marian needed emotional relief; Jasper performs cheerfulness while reading his manuscript.
c30:p29.best_quote: It was as necessary to him as to her to have a respite before the graver discussion began

c19:p120.text:
Having brought himself to this admission, Reardon felt more at ease. To
      what purpose should he keep up transparent pretences? It was manifestly
      his duty to earn as much money as he could, in whatever way. Let the man
      of letters be forgotten; he was seeking for remunerative employment, just
      as if he had never written a line.
c19:p120.summary: Edwin resolves to abandon literary pretence entirely and seek remunerative work, accepting his economic necessity as duty.
c19:p120.best_quote: To what purpose should he keep up transparent pretences? It was manifestly his duty to earn as much money as he could, in whatever way. Let the man of letters be forgotten; he was seeking for remunerative employment, just as if he had never written a line.

c25:p20.text:
He kept one suit of clothes for his hours of attendance at the hospital;
      it was still decent, and with much care would remain so for a long time.
      That which he wore at home and in his street wanderings declared poverty
      at every point; it had been discarded before he left the old abode. In his
      present state of mind he cared nothing how disreputable he looked to
      passers-by. These seedy habiliments were the token of his degradation, and
      at times he regarded them (happening to see himself in a shop mirror) with
      pleasurable contempt. The same spirit often led him for a meal to the
      poorest of eating-houses, places where he rubbed elbows with ragged
      creatures who had somehow obtained the price of a cup of coffee and a
      slice of bread and butter. He liked to contrast himself with these
      comrades in misfortune. ‘This is the rate at which the world esteems me; I
      am worth no better provision than this.’ Or else, instead of emphasising
      the contrast, he defiantly took a place among the miserables of the nether
      world, and nursed hatred of all who were well-to-do.
c25:p20.summary: Reardon's shabby clothes become both a badge of his fall and a source of bitter pleasure; he identifies with the poor and despises the well-to-do, alternating between shame and defiant self-magnification.
c25:p20.best_quote: These seedy habiliments were the token of his degradation, and at times he regarded them (happening to see himself in a shop mirror) with pleasurable contempt

c30:p150.text:
The thick black fog penetrated every corner of the house. It could be
      smelt and tasted. Such an atmosphere produces low-spirited languor even in
      the vigorous and hopeful; to those wasted by suffering it is the very reek
      of the bottomless pit, poisoning the soul. Her face colourless as the
      pillow, Marian lay neither sleeping nor awake, in blank extremity of woe;
      tears now and then ran down her cheeks, and at times her body was shaken
      with a throe such as might result from anguish of the torture chamber.
c30:p150.summary: The narrator evokes the oppressive London fog as a physical manifestation of Marian's emotional anguish; it is almost Dantean in its suggestion of hellish suffering.
c30:p150.best_quote: The thick black fog penetrated every corner of the house. It could be smelt and tasted. Such an atmosphere produces low-spirited languor even in the vigorous and hopeful; to those wasted by suffering it is the very reek of the bottomless pit, poisoning the soul
